mappings.note: Assertion-reason with a FALSE reason: the Sun looks bigger because it is CLOSEST, not because it is the largest star. The student must supply the right cause, LO-135.

Which statements about the Sun hold -- it is a star of hot gases, but Earth revolves around it, not the reverse. Identification of the Sun and its place, LO-131. Only the last of the three numbered statements survives in the stem.
A long-tailed object moving across the sky over nights is a comet. Identification from observable features, LO-131.
The Moon is about 384,000 km away. A measured distance, LO-137.
Why Polaris looks fixed -- it lies near the extended axis of rotation. The item asks for the cause, LO-135.
Nakshatra as the Indian term for a star or star group. A classification of sky objects, LO-133.
The Chandrayaan-3 landing date, now National Space Day. Space science as public achievement; LO-140 is the nearest fit, as the frame has no LO for missions.
Why Earth looks blue from space -- most of its surface is water. The item asks for the cause of an appearance, LO-135.
Which is NOT an ideal sky-watching condition -- a lit city centre. Planning the conditions of an observation, LO-134.
A ladle or plough pattern in the northern sky is the Big Dipper. Identification from an observable pattern, LO-131.
Assertion-reason with a false reason: planets reflect, they do not fuse. Requires the star/planet differentiation on how each shines, LO-132.

Which statements about the Moon hold -- sole satellite, cratered, hardly any atmosphere. Identification by observable features, LO-131. Only the last of the three numbered statements survives in the stem.
A caravan leader finding north without a compass uses the Pole Star. LO-140's register of applying learning to find directions.
Caravans through Nubra navigated by particular stars. Applied direction-finding, LO-140.
Whether stars shine by their own or reflected light. The property that separates stars from planets, LO-132.
Star groups forming patterns are constellations. Naming a class of sky object, LO-133.
The IAU lists 88 constellations. The formal classification of the sky, LO-133.
Sirius, brightest in the night sky, in Canis Major. Identification by an observable feature, LO-131.
The Big Dipper is Saptarishi in India. Naming the same pattern in two traditions, LO-131.
The star fixed in the north is the Pole Star. Identification by observable behaviour, LO-131.
Excess artificial light at night is light pollution. An environmental harm named, LO-141.
Whether Polaris can be seen from the southern hemisphere. The answer follows from where it sits relative to Earth's axis, LO-135.
The Sun is a hot spherical ball of gases. Identification by composition, LO-131.
The Sun-Earth distance is one astronomical unit. A physical quantity with its unit, LO-137.
Motion around the Sun is revolution. Naming a process, LO-136.
Mercury is nearest the Sun. Placing a planet in the ordered set, LO-133.
Mars is the Red Planet. Identification by appearance, LO-131.
Saturn's rings are dust and rocky material. Identification by composition, LO-131.
Natural satellites are moons. Naming a class of body, LO-131.
Earth has one Moon. A count attached to a body, LO-137.
The bowl-like lunar structures are craters. Naming a feature from its appearance, LO-131.
Our home galaxy is the Milky Way, or Akasha Ganga. Placing our system in a larger class, LO-133.
Planets around other stars are exoplanets. Extending the planet classification beyond our system, LO-133.
How star patterns guided people before modern technology. Applying the learning to find directions, LO-140.
The IAU's current definition of a constellation as a REGION of sky. The formal classification, LO-133, distinct from the traditional pattern sense.
Orion the hunter and the three belt stars. Identification from an observable pattern, LO-131.
Why the Pole Star matters for navigation. Applied direction-finding, LO-140.
Why fewer stars show over a city -- light pollution, smoke and dust. An environmental harm and its effect, LO-141.
What the Sun is and why it glows. Identification by composition and behaviour, LO-131.
Why the Sun looks bigger and brighter -- it is nearest. The item asks for the cause, LO-135.
What a planet is and the four inner ones named. Defining and populating a class, LO-133.
Why Venus is the Morning or Evening Star. Identification by when and where it is seen, LO-131.
Why Earth is the Blue Planet -- water covers most of it. The cause of an appearance, LO-135.
General characteristics of the four outer planets -- large, gaseous, ringed. Identification by observable features, LO-131.
Why Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther -- its dense atmosphere traps heat. A phenomenon related to its cause, LO-135; NEP content the frame does not name.
What a natural satellite is, with an example. Defining and populating a class, LO-133.
The Moon's surface and what causes its craters. The item names the feature AND its cause, LO-135.
What the asteroid belt is and where it lies. A named region grouping a class of body, LO-133.
What comets are made of and what causes the tail. The causal half is what the item marks, LO-135.
What makes up the Solar System. Populating the class, LO-133.
What the Milky Way is and how our system relates to it. Placing one class inside another, LO-133.
Why stars are invisible by day -- the Sun's brightness overwhelms them. The item asks for the cause, LO-135.
The significance of Chandrayaan-3's south-pole landing. Space science as achievement; LO-140 is the nearest fit in a frame with no LO for missions.
How constellations served ancient navigators (LO-140) and how the IAU defines them today as sky regions (LO-133). The item explicitly asks for both.
What light pollution is, its effect on observation, and the dark sky reserves created against it. Efforts to protect a shared environmental resource, LO-141.
The Sun's characteristics, why Earth depends on it, and why it looks unlike other stars. The last clause turns on proximity as the cause, LO-135.
The eight planets in order, then DIFFERENTIATE inner from outer on composition and size. The differentiation is the marked half, LO-132.
What moons are plus the Moon's key features. LO-131 for the surface characteristics, LO-137 because distance and revolution period are asked for as quantities.
Asteroids and comets described side by side on composition and where each is found. An explicit differentiation of two classes, LO-132.
The full pointer-star method for finding Polaris (LO-134, the observation procedure) and why it matters for navigation (LO-140).
